_comment: Claims that circulate about the city, checked against the record this site already publishes. Hand-authored, like data.tax-case.json — nothing here is generated, because deciding what a claim actually asserts is not a thing a script can do. The rules the page states in `how` are binding on this file: a claim is only listed when it can be answered out of an open-meeting recording, a document the city or the state published, or arithmetic on figures from one of those, and every entry carries the citation next to the sentence it supports. Claims are quoted as they circulate and never attributed to a private individual by name; officials speaking in an open meeting are named, because that is the record. `verdict` is one of the keys in `verdicts` below. `checked` is when the entry was last read against the record; a claim about a live dispute goes stale quickly, which is why every card prints that date. `summary` is this project's one-line description of what was claimed and is what the card heading and the docket row carry; `claim` stays the wording as it circulates and is printed under the heading, quoted, so the reader can always see which sentence is theirs and which is ours. `topics` are keys from `categories`, which is what the filter bar at the top of the page is built from: the first topic is the heading a claim files under and the rest are the other shelves it belongs on, because most of these claims are about two things at once.
title: What's going around, and what the record says
sub: Things residents are telling each other about the city: the tax increase, the staffing, the petition, all set against the meetings, the notices and the audited figures they can be checked against. Some are true, some are out of date, and the ones the city itself put into circulation get the same treatment as the ones aimed at it.

how.heading: How something gets on this page
rules: It has to be circulating. Not a hypothetical, not a strawman: something being repeated in a comment thread, on a sign, at a hearing, or in the city's own messaging.

It has to be checkable against a source that exists. A recording of an open meeting, a document published by a government body (this city, another one, the county, the state or the federal government), or arithmetic done here on figures from one of those. A claim about how Eagle Mountain compares with anywhere else can only be settled from outside Eagle Mountain, so the sources go where the answer is. If nothing can settle it, the entry says so rather than guessing.
The claim gets quoted; the person doesn't get named. Residents in a comment thread are not public figures. Officials speaking in an open meeting are, and are named.
The city's own claims are checked the same way. Two of the entries below are things the city said, not things said about it.
Every card carries the date it was last checked, because half of these turn on a rate the council has already changed twice.
how.submit: Something being repeated that isn't here? The claim as you heard it, and where you saw it, is enough to start with.

claims.summary: A 220 percent property tax increase
claims.claim: The council raised your property taxes 220 percent.
claims.ruling: 220.88% was noticed in June and never adopted. The rate that survives is 0.000900: 69.81% over the certified rate, on the city's own line, which is about a tenth of a property tax bill.
claims.seen: Yard signs, petition sheets and city Facebook groups, June to August 2026
claims.true_part: The number was real and the city printed it. The Truth-in-Taxation notice mailed in June proposed 0.001700 against a 0.000530 certified rate and stated the increase as 220.88%: a rise in the city's budgeted property tax revenue over the prior year, excluding eligible new growth.
claims.wrong_part: Two things. The figure is three rates out of date: the council adopted 0.001500 on August 6, repealed it on August 18, and adopted 0.000900 in its place. And it was never a percentage of anybody's tax bill (it is a percentage of the city's own levy, which is one of seven lines on an Eagle Mountain bill), the fourth-largest of them on today's bill, and the third once the new rate is levied.
detail: On the notice's own average home ($488,000 of market value, $268,400 taxable after Utah's 55% primary-residence exemption), the noticed rate would have added $314.03 a year. The rate in force adds $99.31.

On that same home the city's line goes from about $143 a year to about $242, inside a total bill of about $2,517 at 2025 rates. That is the city's share moving from roughly 5.7% of the bill to roughly 9.2% of it. Alpine School District's line alone is more than six times the city's.
claims.provisional: The 0.000900 is certain; the vote, the motion and the figures the adopting resolution recites were not published when this was written, so everything priced at that rate here is this project's arithmetic on it.

claims.summary: Every dollar of the increase goes to public safety
claims.claim: Every dollar of the increase goes straight to public safety.
claims.claim_note: The city's own claim, not one aimed at it.
claims.ruling: True in the schedule's own terms: the levy is smaller than the Sheriff's contract, so there is no second dollar to allocate. What it left out is that the money largely replaces sales tax already paying that contract, and frees the sales tax for other things.
claims.seen: City messaging, quoted back to the council at the August 6 hearing
claims.true_part: The statutory impact schedule names the Sheriff's contract as the affected budget and puts it at $9,798,139: the same figure, to the dollar, as the proposed property tax revenue. Designed that way, the levy covers the contract and nothing else.
claims.wrong_part: What actually changes is which pot pays. Property tax takes over a contract sales tax had been subsidizing, and the freed sales tax goes to other city spending: parks, roads, staff. That is a defensible policy and it is not what "every dollar goes to public safety" conveys, which is why residents who did the subtraction, $6.74 million noticed against a $1.5 million rise in the contract, concluded they had been lied to.
detail: At the rate finally adopted the gap runs the other way and is larger. 0.000900 raises about $5.19 million against a contract of $9,798,139, so roughly $4.61 million of the Sheriff's contract still comes out of sales tax, four times what the repealed rate would have left short.

claims.summary: The tax was rushed through in secret
claims.claim: They did this in secret and rushed it through.
claims.ruling: Two different charges are tangled together. On whether it was done in the open the record is unusually complete: eight open meetings from April 14, both August hearings set three months ahead, the schedule read into the record five times. On whether residents found out, the council agrees with the criticism: three of the five said so by name from the dais before voting, and a fourth voice said it in the cross-talk that followed.
claims.seen: Comment threads and hearing testimony, June to August 2026
claims.true_part: Residents did not hear about it in time to weigh in early, and that is not in dispute. The council conceded it on the record before the vote, and the concession is the strongest evidence for the complaint.
claims.wrong_part: Nothing was done outside a noticed public meeting. The Sheriff's Office presented the staffing case in an open work session on April 14; on May 5 the council accepted the tentative budget, acknowledged the proposed increase and declared its intent to exceed the certified rate, setting both August hearings; the mayor read the impact schedule that night, and again on May 26, June 2 and June 16, and the June 16 hearing ran with public comment answered at length. The June 2 reading is recorded in the minutes rather than the recording, which runs out partway through public comment. The August 6 hearing took about sixty speakers over three hours.

claims.summary: The money pays for a city police department
claims.claim: The increase pays for the city's own police department.
claims.ruling: Eagle Mountain employs no police officers and no firefighters. Patrol is bought from the Utah County Sheriff's Office; fire and ambulance come from Unified Fire Authority, which bills residents on a separate line of the same tax notice.
claims.seen: Recurring in comment threads whenever the Sheriff's contract comes up
claims.true_part: The money does pay for policing. The affected budget on the impact schedule is the Sheriff's contract, and the deputies it funds are assigned to the Eagle Mountain division.
claims.wrong_part: It is a contract, not a department. The city's audited schedule shows 4.82 full-time equivalents under public safety and every one of them is a crossing guard; the line for firefighters and officers reads zero, and has read zero in all eleven years that schedule covers. Fire and ambulance are not the city's at all: Unified Fire Service Area levies 0.001650 directly, which is nearly twice the city's own new rate.
detail: This matters for reading a tax bill. Someone comparing Eagle Mountain's rate against a neighboring city that runs its own police and fire is comparing a city that buys those services against one that levies for them, and the neighbor's higher rate is partly that difference.

claims.summary: Signing the petition repeals the tax
claims.claim: Sign the petition and the tax goes away.
claims.ruling: A referendum on a property tax rate is legally available, and one ran in a Utah city as recently as last autumn. But the resolution a petition was organized against was repealed on August 18 and replaced, and the signature test is two thresholds rather than one.
claims.seen: Petition drives and organizing posts, August 2026
claims.true_part: Utah Code § 20A-7-613 exists for exactly this situation. Five sponsors file a notarized application with the resolution attached; the city's budget officer must then produce an unbiased fiscal and legal impact statement within days; then signatures are gathered against a statutory threshold.
claims.wrong_part: Nothing about it is automatic, and two things are unsettled. The first is what a petition aimed at the August 6 resolution does now that the resolution has been repealed and a smaller increase adopted in its place: that turns on what was filed and when, and the city recorder is the authority on it, not this page. The second is the threshold itself.
detail: For a city of the second class it is 8.25% of active voters citywide and 8.25% within at least 75% of the city's voter participation areas. Both must be met, and the second is what decides these. It is the one almost nobody organizing a petition budgets for.

Whether Eagle Mountain is second class yet is itself open. The statutory line is 65,000 residents, the first statewide subcounty estimates put the city at 65,409 in 2025, and the class changes on the lieutenant governor's certificate rather than on the estimate. If that certificate has not issued, the thresholds are 10% rather than 8.25%.

figures.note: of active voters, 10% if still third class

figures.label: And by area
figures.note: of voter participation areas must each clear 8.25%

claims.summary: Another data center is being built
claims.claim: They're building another data center in Eagle Mountain.
claims.ruling: Yes, and the votes are on file. What is being built is more of what is already here: every data center approval in the record since 2024 is an expansion by Meta or QTS, not a new company arriving.
claims.seen: A city Facebook group, August 2026; and public comment to the council since at least February 2026
claims.true_part: Three campuses are already named in the city's own record (Meta, Google and QTS), and building has not stopped. QTS's SLC1 site was still under construction this spring, when the council let it work outside the hours city code normally allows. A second QTS parcel, the land the motion calls QTS-SCL 2, was rezoned on March 3. And on October 21 the council approved a development agreement with Stadion, LLC, the company known as Meta, on a 4–1 vote, along with a third amendment to its water and sewer agreement the same night.
claims.wrong_part: “Another” suggests a new operator. Nothing in the record shows one. It is also worth knowing what has not happened yet: the newest land in play (the parcel west of the Pony Express area that QTS has bought) was described to the council on August 4 as still zoned agricultural. Farmland cannot be built on until the council rezones it, and a rezone is a public vote with a public hearing in front of it.
detail: The scale of it gets overstated in both directions. A resident told the council in February that they had read five more had been approved. In the twelve months before that comment the council passed four measures touching the data centers: a road realignment at the Meta site, the Meta development agreement, the water and sewer amendment beside it, and a sign-code rule for directional signage, and none of the four approved a new data center.

The motions themselves are thin, which is a fair complaint about the record rather than about the claim. The QTS-SCL 2 rezone does not state the acreage or the new zoning, and the Meta development agreement does not list its terms. The votes are public; what was voted on is often summarized in a single line.

claims.summary: It will be the largest data center in the country
claims.claim: It's going to be the largest data center in the country, maybe the world.
claims.ruling: No. A single project already approved in Box Elder County covers 40,000 acres: more ground than the whole of Eagle Mountain, which is 32,256 acres of land. Whatever gets built here, the largest in the country is not going in this city.
claims.seen: A city Facebook group, August 2026, in a thread about the new site
claims.true_part: The premise underneath it is sound. Eagle Mountain has three data center campuses, it keeps approving work on them, and QTS has bought more ground west of the Pony Express area that has not been through the council yet. Somebody hearing that a company is buying more land here is hearing something true, and the state as a whole is getting enormous ones.
claims.wrong_part: It is the superlative that fails, and it fails on a comparison anyone can make. The Stratos project area in western Box Elder County, a data and energy campus approved by the MIDA board on April 24 and agreed to by the Box Elder County Commission on May 4, covers 40,000 acres. Eagle Mountain City is 50.4 square miles of land, which is 32,256 acres. The project area 200 miles north is about a quarter larger than this entire city, and it is the one Utah newsrooms have been calling the largest in the country.
detail: Two honest qualifications, neither of which rescues the claim. The 40,000 acres is the project area rather than the buildings: the state's own FAQ says most of it will stay undeveloped and the data center footprint will be “a fraction” of it. And those April and May votes created the project area, not the project: the state says plainly that they did not approve the full development, which still needs air, water and wildlife review.

The other half of the problem is local, and it is the more useful half. Nothing Eagle Mountain has voted on states a size for anything. The QTS-SCL 2 rezone does not give the acreage or the zoning it granted; the Meta development agreement does not list its terms. So there is no figure in the city's record that a claim about size could be measured against, which is exactly why a superlative can circulate here for weeks without meeting a number.

claims.summary: A $150 million tax break for the data centers
claims.claim: You gave the data centers a $150 million tax break and now you are asking residents to pay.
claims.ruling: The break is real and the council was a party to it, but the $150 million was granted by five taxing entities together and Eagle Mountain City's own line is about six cents of every dollar, roughly $9 million of it. What the claim leaves out cuts both ways: the deals struck since 2018 are worth several times $150 million, and the city's share of the newest one alone is larger than twenty years of the tax increase.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026; and twice in public comment at the 6 August hearing
claims.true_part: The 2018 deal is in the city's own minutes, in plain language. On 15 May 2018 the council adopted the Sweetwater Industrial Park Community Reinvestment Area #1 plan for a 487-acre data center, and staff told it exactly what the company had asked for: 80% of the real property taxes and 100% of the personal property taxes returned to it, against an investment of $750 million. The vote was unanimous (Burnham, Clark, Curtis, Gricius and Reaves), and the same evening the term in the interlocal agreement was changed from twenty years to forty. Melissa Clark, who voted for it, was on the dais for the 6 August hearing. Nor did it stop there: the council adopted Sweetwater #2 in March 2021, #3 in April 2023, and #4 on 5 November 2025 by four votes to one.
claims.wrong_part: The $150 million was never the city's to spend. Five taxing entities signed those interlocals, and the only per-entity splits the city has ever published, the hearing notices for project areas #3 and #4, put Eagle Mountain City at 6.3% and 6.0% of the money, against 63% for Alpine School District. At that share the city's part of a $150 million break is about $9 million spread across the life of the agreement. And it is increment rather than cash: it is levied on value that did not exist before, on ground the 2018 minutes record as paying $66 a year in property tax across all entities, $6 of it Eagle Mountain's.
detail: Two details in the version spoken at the hearing are worth separating. The percentage is not the 77% quoted from the floor; the minutes state 80% of the real property tax and 100% of the personal property tax. The forty years is right, and it is the part most worth knowing: the request was presented to the council as a twenty-year incentive, and the interlocal was amended to forty the same night, which is the maximum state law allows.

The counterweight is audited and sits in the city's own annual report. Stadion, LLC, the company known as Meta, is the largest property taxpayer in Eagle Mountain at $305,404,041 of taxable value, 15.63% of everything taxable in the city, and that is with 80% of its real property rebated. In the year to 30 June 2024 the Redevelopment Agency took in $9,746,126 of Sweetwater increment and paid $9,546,141 of it back out.

The strongest version of this argument is bigger than the number it is usually made with, and the city published it itself. Eagle Mountain's own line on project area #4 (noticed in January at $778,540,678 across the five entities) is $46,857,489, which is about twenty-two years of what the new rate raises above the certified rate. Against that sits what the same notice says of the same money: it is generated “only if the Project Area is developed”. Whether these buildings would have gone up without the incentive is the argument, and it is not something the record can settle.

claims.summary: The tax is really about the rodeo grounds
claims.claim: The public safety reason was misleading — the tax increase is really to cover up his misdeeds on the rodeo grounds and build their new kingdom.
claims.ruling: There is a new $1 million rodeo-grounds line in the budget, so the question is a fair one to ask. The increase cannot be what pays for it: at the rate in force the whole city levy falls about $4.6 million short of the city's own public safety budget.

claims.claim_note: “Misdeeds” refers to allegations made in a lawsuit filed against the city in March 2026. The city has formally denied them and no court has ruled on them. The filing and the city's denial are both cited below.

claims.summary: A developer was let out of building the rodeo grounds
claims.claim: The developer was supposed to build the rodeo grounds out in Pole Canyon, and the city let them out of it.
claims.ruling: The promise was real, it was in a signed contract, and it had a date on it: about twenty acres of public rodeo grounds, built and dedicated by June 1, 2015. The city did release it: nine weeks after residents stood at the podium and asked the council to enforce it. What the claim leaves out is that the release was a noticed agenda item carried 3–2 with two members voting no, and that the city took something in exchange each time it gave ground.
claims.seen: Public comment and public hearing, Eagle Mountain City Council, March 18, 2014
claims.claim_note: This is on the page now because the FY2026–27 budget carries $1,000,000 to relocate the rodeo grounds, which puts the question of who was supposed to build them in the first place back in front of residents.
claims.true_part: Section 8.2 of the Pole Canyon Annexation and Master Development Agreement, dated January 19, 2010 and signed under Mayor Heather Jackson, required the Pole Canyon Investment Group to subdivide and dedicate to the city a parcel of approximately twenty acres as a public rodeo grounds, and to build it by the earlier of the date the property's aggregate market value reached $250 million or June 1, 2015. It specified the facility down to the fittings: a rodeo-equipped arena, holding pens, bleachers for 500, a warm-up pen, lighting, restrooms and concessions, capable of hosting a high school rodeo. On July 1, 2014 the city deleted that section in its entirety. The deadline has never come back.
claims.wrong_part: It was not done quietly, and it was not done for nothing. The council took the First Amendment up as item 16 on the noticed May 20, 2014 agenda and adopted it 3–2: Burnham, Steinkopf and Westmoreland in favor, Bradley and Ireland against. In place of the deadline the developer paid $90,000 for publicly owned bleachers and still owed at least twenty acres as a regional park, and in 2016 that was traded again for at least one hundred acres of recreational land. The framing also skips who was in the room: the president of the rodeo committee who negotiated the bleacher purchase across the dais that night was Jared Gray, later the mayor.
detail: The rodeo Eagle Mountain has actually had since 2010 was the interim facility. Section 8.3 required the developer to provide, by May 1, 2010, a temporary arena at the existing Pony Express Park for use until the permanent Pole Canyon grounds were finished. On March 30, 2010 the council bought the arena equipment for $98,369.20 on a 4–1 vote, with DAI, the Pole Canyon developer, repaying $107,000 of it against its obligation under the agreement, and the minutes record that the equipment “could be relocated to the proposed Pole Canyon rodeo arena site when it was ready”. The First Amendment declared section 8.3 fulfilled.

The amendment the city published is not quite the amendment the council voted for. Councilmember Burnham's motion approved the First Amendment with wording added into section 8.2.2 fixing development to the date the property's market value reached $250 million, with the word “consider” struck, and subject to a rodeo grounds operation, management and lease agreement with the rodeo committee. The signed copy stamped by the City Recorder's office carries none of the three: 8.2.2 has no date and no market-value trigger, and the city still only agrees to “consider” putting the park in its impact fee plan.

By 2016 the rodeo grounds were gone from the agreement altogether. The Second Amendment, effective April 19, 2016, replaced section 8.2 again, “in lieu of any requirement relating to the dedication or construction of any public rodeo grounds”, with at least 100 acres for a Boy Scout high adventure camp, a wake park and a trail system. In July 2023 the whole 2010 agreement was novated and superseded by the Firefly Amended and Restated Master Development Agreement, which mentions rodeo grounds once, as a permitted land use.

Residents saw it coming. On March 18, 2014, two months before the vote, a White Hills resident told the council that the developer had promised rodeo grounds when Pole Canyon and White Hills were annexed and asked the elected officials to hold him to it; another said that if the city had held the developer to the agreement the rodeo would not be a problem, because a rodeo grounds was to be built as part of it; a third told the public hearing that the agreement promised a rodeo facility in Pole Canyon by 2015 and that the council had failed to require it.

claims.summary: A $5.5 million gift was spent on a road
claims.claim: QTS gave 5.5 million dollars to help citizens and the mayor decided to use those funds to fix a road.
claims.ruling: There was no $5.5 million gift. Two figures spoken on the same night have been fused: QTS agreed to pay the roughly $5 million cost of widening Pony Express Parkway, and $5,591,594 was the new revenue from the tax rate the council adopted hours later.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026
claims.true_part: QTS did commit money, and the mayor did ask for it. On August 6 Mayor Gray told the hearing that the city had been trying to work out how to widen Pony Express Parkway, that he phoned QTS to propose a reimbursement agreement, and that they came back offering to pay the entire bill rather than the half he had asked for.
claims.wrong_part: It was road money in the sentence it was first mentioned. There were never general funds sitting there to be redirected. And the $5.5 million in circulation is a different number from the same meeting: the net revenue above the certified rate that a rate of 0.001500 would raise, $5,591,594, which finance staff computed during the deliberation and which was read into the adopting motion. That rate was repealed twelve days later.
detail: The mayor's stated reason for making the call is the same argument the post makes: that traffic generated by the data center's workers should not be a burden carried by residents.

The wider corridor work is not city property tax either. The Ranches Parkway and Pony Express project discussed on August 4 runs on MAG regional funding, with the city cash-flowing parts of it against a reimbursement interlocal. Staff put the design and construction at $11.4 million that night, and the programmed figure at $11.8 million in current dollars, $13.8 million as MAG budgets it for 2030.

I said, it's about a $5 million bill with 2 stoplights… not only will we help, we'll pay for that entire $5 million bill.

claims.summary: Big Tech should have bonded for the road
claims.claim: Big Tech should have bonded for that road from the beginning.
claims.ruling: A fair criticism with a real fact behind it, the council did cut what commercial builders pay toward roads. It ends with the data center funding the whole project anyway.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026
claims.true_part: On February 18, 2025 the council voted unanimously, Gray among them, to partially suspend the transportation impact fee for nonresidential development, and removed the restaurant carve-out at every building size. The city chose to charge commercial building less toward roads, and that is the strongest fact available to anyone arguing large employers under-contributed.
claims.wrong_part: The framing assumes a bond was available and refused. Utah cities cannot set a separate tax rate for data centers, and a councilmember told the August 6 hearing the city already charges the maximum impact fees state law allows. What the city got instead was QTS funding the full cost of the widening, and declining incentives it had already been granted on its next two buildings, more than a bond would have guaranteed on this particular road.

claims.summary: No bond was required for Pony Express Parkway
claims.claim: Why didn't the city make big tech bond for Pony Express since they were going to ruin it from driving on it?
claims.ruling: Put as a failure that already happened. The company is funding the entire project, and a bond is not the instrument that does this job.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026
claims.true_part: The corridor is the city's biggest cost problem, and residents are right that it has been paid for locally for years. In May 2019 the council approved a UDOT Transportation Infrastructure Fund loan of up to $2,000,000 for widening Pony Express Parkway, and further work ran through 2024 and 2025.
claims.wrong_part: A subdivision improvement bond guarantees that a developer finishes and warranties roads inside its own project, so the city is not left with an unfinished street. There is nothing to guarantee completion of when an existing employer's staff drive an existing public arterial. The lawful tools there are impact fees and negotiated reimbursement or participation agreements, and a reimbursement agreement is what the mayor said he opened the QTS call by proposing. The result was QTS paying the whole bill.

claims.summary: Thirty years of impact fees for Pony Express
claims.claim: The Waldens built Pony Express 30 years ago. The city has been collecting impact fees for 30 years for that road.
claims.ruling: The founding half is right in substance. The impact fee half describes something Utah law does not permit: a fee has to be spent or committed within six years, not banked for thirty.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026
claims.true_part: The founding is a matter of record. John Walden and two partners bought roughly 8,000 acres in Cedar Valley in 1994; the town of Eagle Mountain incorporated on December 3, 1996 and became a city in 2001. The original parkway came out of that development, and “thirty years” is close enough to right.
claims.wrong_part: Impact fees cannot accumulate that way. Utah's Impact Fees Act requires a city to spend or encumber an impact fee within six years of collecting it, and only on a system improvement named in the impact fee facilities plan for that fee type; holding longer requires a written finding of an extraordinary and compelling reason and a date certain. Nor is it one continuous fee: Eagle Mountain tabled an updated transportation impact fee twice in May 2020, adopted the update on March 6, 2024, and partially suspended the fee for nonresidential building on February 18, 2025. And for the first two of those thirty years there was no city to collect anything.

sources.speaker: Utah Impact Fees Act
sources.note: A local political subdivision shall expend or encumber an impact fee for a permissible use within six years of collecting it, and may expend impact fees only for a system improvement identified in the impact fee facilities plan for the public facility type the fee was collected for.

doc.title: Utah Code § 11-36a-602 — expenditure of impact fees

sources.speaker: Councilmember Wright, moving the updated transportation impact fee
sources.note: The ordinance adopting an updated impact fee enactment for the transportation impact fee. The same update was tabled on 5 May and again on 19 May 2020; the fee was partially suspended for nonresidential building on 18 February 2025.

claims.summary: Developers are made to bond for roads
claims.claim: They make builders and developers bond for roads that they could potentially ruin all the time!
claims.ruling: True, and it describes a different instrument doing a different job from the one the post wants it to do.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026
claims.true_part: Cities do require this constantly, Eagle Mountain included. A subdivision improvement bond is posted as a condition of plat approval and guarantees that the developer builds, completes and warranties the roads inside its own project, so the city is not left holding an unfinished street if the builder walks away. The record carries bond releases as routine consent items.
claims.wrong_part: The posture does not transfer. An operating employer whose staff drive an existing public arterial has no obligation to build to guarantee. The lawful ways to make growth pay for road capacity are impact fees, which a councilmember told the August 6 hearing the city already charges at the statutory maximum, and negotiated reimbursement or participation agreements, which is the route that produced the QTS commitment.

claims.summary: A city jail would be a revenue source
claims.claim: Jared should have used 5.5 to build a new jail. Then we would have a revenue source and be able to ticket for city laws and keep all the money from fines instead of giving it to Utah County.
claims.ruling: Right that fine money is going to the county. Wrong about the building that fixes it (that is a justice court, not a jail), and wrong about the scale, which is thousands of dollars, not millions.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026
claims.true_part: The underlying complaint is real, and councilmembers agree with it. Eagle Mountain has no justice court, and its ordinances are not loaded in the system the county justice court files charges from, so charges for city-ordinance violations cannot even be brought. A councilmember said on April 14, 2026 that the city had been talking about a justice court “for over 18 months and we're nowhere closer to it.”
claims.wrong_part: Three things. There was no $5.5 million to spend; see the QTS entry. A jail is not the mechanism: what lets a city keep fines from its own ordinances is a justice court, and in Utah the sheriff is the statutory keeper of the county jail, with the nearest booking facility in Spanish Fork. And the money is not there: the entire budgeted general-fund Fines line for FY2026–27 is $6,180, against $9,798,139 of budgeted public safety. A city jail is a cost center with staffing, medical care and liability attached, not a revenue line.
detail: The city attorney told the council on May 26, 2026 that the city is “legally entitled” to a justice court and that what stands in the way is process, not money for a building.
The broader “Fines & Forfeitures” category citywide, $157,700 in the FY2025–26 budget book, is mostly NSF fees, library fines, code enforcement fines and late utility charges, not traffic citations.

claims.summary: A councilman said the city has no money
claims.claim: Brett Wright talked about how broke the city is and how there is NO MONEY.
claims.ruling: Not what the recording has him saying. His argument that night was about choices and about not standing for re-election, not about an empty account.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026
claims.true_part: Wright did speak at length about the city's finances at the August 6 hearing, and the council as a body did argue that the current revenue mix is not holding. He seconded the motion that set the rate.
claims.wrong_part: What he actually said was that the easy path would have been to do nothing and keep cutting services, and that he is in his fifth year and will not run again. His stated reason for voting without an electoral calculation in it. The council's case was structural rather than “no money”: sales tax is being consumed by the sheriff's contract, leaving intersections without signals; sales tax collapses in a downturn and the need for police does not; and Councilmember Wood put the city's share of the master transportation plan at $419 million by 2035. Residents in the same room argued the opposite, that the city already has the money.
detail: The transcript of this meeting is now speaker-attributed, so the remarks above can be read against his name rather than inferred. The chair hands off to each member by name before they speak (“Okay, thank you. Councilmember Wright, go ahead”), and Wright's reply runs from there to “My time's about out, but thank you for being here.” Nothing in it says the city has no money.

The later open deliberation is a different matter: after about 03:42 members interrupt each other and the chair stops introducing anyone, so that stretch is left unattributed on the site rather than guessed. The second quotation below sits in that stretch, which is why it is credited to a councilmember and not to a named one.

figures.note: seconded the rate motion, then said he will not run again

sources.quote: We have intersections that are missing traffic control signals because we can't afford to put them in. Where does that money come from? If we continue to pull sales tax dollars, which could fund those infrastructure improvements, and we continue to allocate it to our sheriff's contract…

claims.summary: The city should own its utilities and its police
claims.claim: Build a revenue source. Like owning your own utilities or owning your own police officers.
claims.ruling: The city already owns its utilities, on a scale six times its general fund. And city-funded policing is exactly what the tax increase pays for: the same policy this post's opening sentence calls a cover story, though the city buys it under contract rather than employing it.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026
claims.true_part: Both are sound instincts about municipal finance, and the second one is city policy. Eagle Mountain employs no police officers today: patrol is bought from the Utah County Sheriff's Office, and fire and ambulance come from Unified Fire Authority, which bills residents on a separate line of the same tax notice.
claims.wrong_part: The utilities half describes something that has been true for years. Eagle Mountain runs water, sewer, storm drain and solid waste as city-owned funds, plus an internal utility billing fund; in FY2026–27 those total roughly $269.7 million against a $42.7 million general fund: a gap that is mostly one year's borrowing, because the sewer fund alone jumps from $17.5 million to $217.5 million on the up to $230,000,000 of water and sewer revenue bonds the council authorized on February 17, 2026. The police half is the increase itself, and what it buys is a contract rather than a department. A post cannot call public safety a pretext in its first line and propose city-owned police as the alternative in its ninth.
detail: Municipal utilities in Utah are also rate-funded enterprises, not general revenue: an enterprise fund charges users for the service and is expected to cover its own costs, which is why a water fund cannot subsidize a police department.

figures.note: water, sewer, storm drain, solid waste, billing

claims.summary: The mayor is shopping for new rodeo grounds
claims.claim: And Jared has been out asking everyone he can for new RODEO GROUNDS, I heard.
claims.ruling: A new rodeo grounds is a real, funded, adopted city project, and a mayor pursuing one would be doing his job. Whether Jared Gray has personally been asking anyone for a site is a different question, and the record does not answer it.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026
claims.wrong_part: None of that is evidence that he has. The claim is about one named person doing a specific thing, and everything above it is about a council decision and a budget line, a different subject. Nothing in the agendas, minutes or recordings shows Jared Gray approaching anyone about a site, and nothing in them rules it out: private calls do not appear in the record this page checks against. His one recorded act on the item is an abstention, while Wright, Burnham, Clark and Wood voted yes, and that is not the rebuttal it looks like, since standing aside is the ordinary response to a declared interest rather than proof there is none. The sourcing offered is “I heard.”
detail: What would settle it: a site named in an agenda, a property owner on the record, correspondence released under GRAMA, or the mayor answering the question in an open meeting. None of those exists yet.

claims.true_part: The thing he is said to be shopping for exists. On April 15, 2025 the council adopted a resolution expressing intent to work with the West Traverse Sentinel Landscape committee on relocating the rodeo grounds into the Army Compatible Use Buffer around Camp Williams; the FY2026–27 capital schedule carries $1,000,000 for it; and staff still listed “rodeo grounds planning” among the year's open projects on August 4, 2026. Finding a site means talking to people who own land, so the behavior described is plausible, and, for an adopted project, unremarkable.

claims.summary: A free repair of the eagle monument was ignored
claims.claim: I offered to fix the eagle by 73 for free since it was ours and was never called back. The city could have saved money.
claims.ruling: A private offer and an unreturned phone call leave no trace in an open-meeting record, so this site cannot settle it either way. What can be checked is what happened to the monument.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026
claims.true_part: The eagle monument was down, it mattered to people, and the city spent money putting it back. On May 19, 2026 one voice on the dais said of the monument, “I really didn't know that people cared that much”, and another finished the thought: “until it was gone.”
claims.wrong_part: Nothing is contradicted, and nothing is confirmed. Offers made by phone do not appear in agendas, minutes or recordings, which are the only things this page checks claims against. It would be settled by a written offer or by the city's correspondence: a records request, not a meeting recording.
detail: What the record does carry: by April 28, 2026 city staff had rebuilt the retaining wall and the contractor had poured the footings and pad, with installation scheduled for around the end of May. It was named as one of the few capital projects expected to finish without rolling into the next year.
